interviewQuestions.question: Design a real-time fraud detection system for card transactions.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this as extreme-imbalance binary classification — fraud is typically well under 1% of transactions, so accuracy is meaningless and the real conversation is precision vs recall.

For features, I'd lean heavily on velocity (transaction frequency spikes vs the user's normal pattern) and graph features (is this card/device/address linked to known fraud rings), since a single transaction's raw fields rarely look suspicious in isolation.

For serving, I'd run two speeds: a lightweight real-time model scoring every transaction in milliseconds to block/allow/challenge at checkout, plus a slower batch model with richer features re-scoring recent transactions for human review. I'd flag label latency as a real constraint — confirmed fraud (chargebacks) can take 30-90 days, so the freshest transactions in any training set are exactly the ones without confirmed labels yet.

I'd set the operating threshold as a business trade-off, not a fixed statistical default — comparing the dollar cost of missed fraud against the cost of a false decline, with the risk team, not model metrics alone. And I'd close on adversarial adaptation: fraudsters actively change behavior in response to what gets blocked, so this needs continuous retraining and monitoring, not a train-once-and-deploy model.

**Testing:** whether you recognize fraud's specific structural challenges — imbalance, delayed labels, and an adaptive adversary — rather than treating it like a standard classification problem.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fraud detection system design

interviewQuestions.question: Why does fraud detection need a real-time model AND a separate batch model instead of just one good model running everywhere?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The two speeds exist because they're solving genuinely different constrained problems, and no single model configuration can satisfy both constraints at once. The real-time model has to make a block/allow/challenge decision within a strict latency SLA — the checkout flow is actively waiting on this decision, often within a budget measured in tens of milliseconds — which forces it to use a smaller feature set (only what's cheaply computable in real time) and a simpler, faster model architecture, accepting that it will miss some fraud that needs richer signal to catch.

The batch model has no such time pressure — it runs after the transaction has already completed, re-scoring recent activity — so it can afford genuinely expensive features that take longer to compute (graph-based signals about whether this device or card links to a broader fraud ring, aggregated velocity patterns across a longer window, ensembles of multiple models) and can catch fraud the real-time model's necessarily-limited feature set missed. The trade-off is that whatever the batch model catches, it catches *after* the transaction already happened — it feeds fraud/risk teams for human review and chargeback prevention, not a checkout-blocking decision.

Running only the expensive batch-style model everywhere would blow the checkout latency budget; running only the fast real-time model everywhere would forfeit meaningfully better detection that's only computationally available with more time. The two-speed architecture is specifically an answer to "how much fraud can I catch" split by "how much time do I actually have to catch it in this context."

**Testing:** whether you can justify the two-speed architecture from the actual latency-vs-feature-richness trade-off, rather than just naming that both exist.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why fraud detection needs two model speeds

interviewQuestions.question: Your fraud model's precision has been steadily dropping for three months even though you haven't changed the model or the code. What's your leading hypothesis, and how do you confirm it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My leading hypothesis is adversarial adaptation — fraud is one of the few ML problems where the underlying data distribution actively shifts *in response* to what you've deployed, because the population you're scoring includes an adversary that notices which patterns get blocked and deliberately changes tactics to avoid them. A model that was well-calibrated three months ago can degrade purely because fraudsters have shifted their behavior around its known blind spots, with zero code or model changes on your end — this is structurally different from ordinary data drift, where the shift is incidental rather than deliberately targeting your specific defenses.

To confirm this rather than just assume it, I'd look for the concrete signature: are false negatives (fraud that slipped through) clustering around specific feature patterns that used to be reliable fraud signals but have recently stopped correlating as strongly with confirmed fraud labels — for instance, if a velocity-based signal that used to catch rapid-fire card testing is now seeing fraudsters deliberately space out transactions to stay under that threshold. I'd also check whether new fraud is concentrating in a segment the model has historically underperformed on, which would suggest fraudsters have found and are exploiting a specific weak spot rather than fraud broadly getting harder to detect.

Given confirmed labels lag by 30-90 days (chargebacks, disputes), I'd also rule out a simpler explanation first: is the recent "precision drop" actually just an artifact of looking at a window where labels haven't fully resolved yet, understating true precision temporarily rather than reflecting a real degradation? Once that's ruled out, the fix for genuine adversarial drift is continuous retraining on the freshest confirmed-label data available and adding monitoring specifically for emerging attack patterns, not a one-time model update — the adversary will adapt to whatever you deploy next too.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish adversarial drift from an artifact of label latency, and know the fix is continuous retraining/monitoring, not a single corrective patch.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing a slow precision decline
